JUDGMENT
This case has arisen as a result of the complainant filing a complaint against the accused under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
The relevant facts required to adjudicate this case are as follows:

The complainant is a proprietorship concern represented by its proprietor and the accused purchased Live Bird Chicken through complainant and at the time of delivering the chicken birds, delivery challan with invoice was given by the complainant.
The accused had purchased these Live Bird Chicken on credit basis.
He was due to an amount of Rs.25,10,304/-.
Towards the discharge of this liability he issued a cheque bearing No.444442 dated 09.09.2019 for Rs.27,10,304, drawn on ICICI Bank, HRBR 3rd block Kalyan Nagar branch, Bengaluru.
When the cheque was presented, it was dishonoured for "Funds Insufficient".
Therefore, a legal notice was issued to the accused which was served upon him.
The C.C.No.2079/2020 accused neither paid the amount nor replied to it.
Hence, this complaint.
3. On presentation of the complaint, the cognizance for the offence was taken.
Pursuant to the issuance of the summons, the accused made appearance before this court and the accused is on bail throughout the trial.
4. On compliance of Section 207 of Cr.P.C, the plea was recorded.

The accused pleaded not guilty,
claimed defense.

5. The Complainant has examined himself as PW.1 and the documents Ex.P1 to Ex.P10 are marked.
The statement of the accused u/S 313 statement was recorded.
The accused has denied all the incriminating evidence against him.
The C.C.No.2079/2020 accused examined himself as DW.1 and Ex.D1 and D3 through Pw1 by confronting these documents.
6. I have given a careful consideration to the arguments advanced by the counsel for both sides.
I have carefully perused the records.
7. In view of the materials placed on record, The following points arise for my consideration 1.
Is there a legally recoverable debt?
2. Whether the complainant proves that the accused has committed the offence punishable under section 138 of N.I.Act?
3. What Order?

8. My findings for the above points are:
Point No.1 : In the Affirmative C.C.No.2079/2020 Point No.2: In the Affirmative Point No.3: As per the final order for the following REASONS 9.
POINT No.1: PW.1 deposes that he is the SPA Holder of the complainant.
The SPA is marked at Ex.P9.

The PW.1 further testifies that the accused purchased living chicken birds from the complainant on various dates and delivery challan with invoice was given to the accused as and when he purchased the chicken birds.

The accused was due for an amount of Rs.25,10,304/-
towards the discharge of this liability the accused has issued the Ex.P1 cheque.
10. The accused admits the cheque and the signature therein.
At this juncture, I rely upon the dictum of Hon'ble Apex Court in Rangappa V/s C.C.No.2079/2020 Mohan reported in 2010(11) SCC 441.

entities.text: Rangappa V/s C.C.No.2079/2020 Mohan reported in 2010(11) SCC 441
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Hon'ble Apex court has held that once the cheque relates to the account of accused and he accepts and admits the signature on the said cheque, then the initial presumption as contemplated under Sec.139 of N.I.Act has to be raised by the court in favour of the complainant.
Of course, this is a rebuttable presumption, and the accused may assert a defence in which the existence of a legally binding obligation or debt is disputed.

It was held at Para 14 as under:
"14....................Keeping this in view, it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139, the standard of proof for doing so is that of `preponderance of probabilities'.
Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the C.C.No.2079/2020 prosecution can fail.

As clarified in the citations, the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own."

3 11.

As the presumption is raised, the onus shifts on the accused to prove that the cheque was not issued to the complainant in discharge of a legally recoverable debt or probabalise his defence as he takes on the hilt of preponderance of probabilities.

12. It is the defence of the accused that though he had purchased chicken birds from the complainant one Sunder Babu who was working with the complainant permitted to provide the chicken birds with a discount of 10% from the market value.
Therefore agreeing to this condition he had purchased the chicken birds.
Thus he is not C.C.No.2079/2020 due to the amount as mentioned in Ex.P1.
In other words the legally recoverable debt outstanding as on the date of Ex.P1 is not the amount so mentioned in it but less than that.
13. It is his another defence that Ex.P1 was issued to the complainant as a security purpose.
It is also his defence that he has paid the entire amount in cash to the complainant.
Now let me go through the oral and documentary evidence adduced by the parties and analyse whether the accused has succeeded in rebutting the presumption.
Promise at a discount price:
14. Needless to state that the accused admits his cheque and the signature therein and also he does not dispute regarding the purchase of the chicken from the complainant.
He says that the C.C.No.2079/2020 manager of the complainant by name Sunder Babu promised to sell the chicken birds at a 10% discount.
I have perused the case papers once again carefully.
During the course of cross examination I do not find any useful material to have been elicited from the mouth of PW.1 regarding this promised discount.

In fact I find no suggestions to have been made to the PW.1 that Sunder Babu had promised to sell the chicken bird on behalf of the complainant at a discount of 10%
from the market price.
That apart no documents are produced before this court by the accused to show that such an offer was made.
15. On the contrary Ex.D3, a complaint lodged before XIX Addl Chief Judicial Magistrate under sec.406, 408, 420, 422 r/w Sec.34 of IPC is produced.
It is instituted to initiate criminal action C.C.No.2079/2020 against Sunder Babu for unauthorized approval of purchase on credit basis.
Two significant aspects are missing.
Firstly, the absence of any documentary evidence indicating that the Manager of the complainant firm had agreed to sell the chicken birds at discounted rates.

Secondly,
the fact that Sunder Babu, who could potentially corroborate this claim, was not summoned as a witness by the accused.
This suggests a lack of corroborative evidence and raises questions about the credibility of the claim regarding the discount sale.

16. It is the vehement argument of the counsel for the accused that the complainant, through Ex.D3,
has previously filed a complaint against Sunder Babu seeking recovery of a due amount, and now the complainant has also filed C.C.No.2079/2020 this subsequent complaint seeking recovery of the amount from the accused.
I have gone through the Ex.D3 carefully.
Both counsels submit that the said case proceedings marked at Ex.D3 is still pending.
On perusal of Ex.D3 it is clear that criminal proceedings initiated is for the offences of cheating, criminal breach of trust.

Though the details of the amount out standing against the accused in the present case is also mentioned in Ex.D3 yet no Golden Fresh vs Waheed Pasha on 9 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/29340682/
4 criminal action is taken against this accused in Ex.D3.

sentences.text: 17 . Para-4 and Para-7 of the complaint marked at Ex.D3 reflects that the said Sunder Babu and Pramod had given approval for the sale of birds on credit basis without obtaining a formal approval from the Manager of the complainant.
The outstanding amount from various customers are C.C.No.2079/2020 also listed down in the said complaint.
The name of the accused and also the amount so outstanding in the present case is also forthcoming in Ex.D.3.
Merely because, the outstanding amount is mentioned in the said Ex.D3, solely can not be a basis to dismiss this complaint under sec.138 of the N.I Act.
At no stretch of this imagination these two complaints stand on same strata.
The question of double jeopardy also does not arise.
Therefore the arguments of the counsel for the accused holds no water.

AMOUNT REPAID:
18.
It is the defence of the accused that he has repaid the amount in cash.

The relevant portion of the cross examination wherein the accused states that he had paid the entire amount by way of cash to Sunder Babu is at page-14, line-6:
C.C.No.2079/2020 "It is the false to suggest that the company is aware of the fact that Sundar Babu received the cash payment from the chicken shop traders including the accused."

The Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in Smt. Parvathamma v/s Smt. Chandrakala in Criminal Appeal No. 508 Of 2015 dated 15.06.2024 has held that when the cheque and its signature is admitted a legal presumption has to be necessarily raised that the cheque was issued for a legally recoverable debt.

When the accused raises a defence that he had borrowed a lesser amount than cheque amount and he has repaid the amount so borrowed, the onus will be on the accused to show that he had in fact borrowed the lesser amount.
19. No doubt the onus is upon the accused to show that he has repaid the entire amount.

If at all,
C.C.No.2079/2020 he had paid the entire amount to the complainant or Sunder Babu as suggested by him during the course of cross-examination, the accused should have produced either the document before this court reflecting the payment of the entire amount or he should have called upon Sunder Babu as his witnesses.
Since no documents are produced, there is no concrete proof to support the claim that the accused has repaid the money.

20. That apart if at all, the accused had repaid the entire amount I am unable to understand what prevented the accused from issuing a legal notice in the return of the cheque, if the complainant had not return the cheque to approach the jurisdictional police, for the behavior of the complainant or to approach the Jurisdictional Magistrate and lodge a complaint or requesting the bank nature of honour C.C.No.2079/2020 the cheque.
No such exercise has been made by the accused in the represent case.

5 21.
However, to substantiate the due amount, the complainant has produced Ex.P10.
It is the ledger extract pertaining to the accused.
Although the ledger extracts were produced as evidence, the accused did not question PW.1 about the contents or details of these documents.
This implies that the authenticity or the significance of the ledger extracts was not challenged through cross- examination.
22. The complainant rely upon Ex.P8 also to show that the accused had agreed to repay the amount as mentioned in Ex.P1.
The accused disputes the execution of Ex.P8.

Para-2 line 7 of the cross examination of DW.1 reflects this :
C.C.No.2079/2020
I have gone through Ex.P8 in the light of the nature of the proceedings and the cross examination made on it.
In this proceeding under sec.138 of the N.I Act, the main document will certainly be ExP1 i.e., cheque.
All other documents would act as a corroboration for the due amount.

Even if Ex.P8 is not considered for a while, upon the defence of the accused that he had repaid the entire amount for the purchase of chicken birds makes this court to shift onus upon the accused to probabalize his defence.
Further the significance of the Ex.P8 would be less in the light of the C.C.No.2079/2020 production of the ledger extract and the cheque, signature having been admitted.
24. Apart from the self serving testimony of the accused, I do not find any evidence on record which would rebut the evidential burden.
The presumption still haunts the accused.
Therefore, I am of the opinion that the rebuttal evidence does not appear to be convinving and acceptable.

25. If all the above evidence is considered as a whole in the light of the above reported judgment, on the hilt of preponderance of probablities, I find from the specs of a common prudent man that the defence theory seems to be improbable, unacceptable.
The presumption raised in favour of the complainant still haunts the accused.
The legally recoverable debt stands probabilised.
Hence, I answer the point No.1 in the C.C.No.2079/2020 AFFIRMATIVE.
26. Point No.2:
The Cheque is dated 09.09.2019.
Ex.P2 shows that Ex.P1 was dishonoured on 29.11.2019 for Funds Insufficient.
A legal notice was issued within the statutory period on 04.12.2019.
The complaint is presented on 20.01.2020.

The complaint is in time and the complainant has complied with all the requirements of the section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
27.
On the basis of the entire materials on record, I am of the opinion that the accused has committed an offence under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
Accordingly I answer the POINT NO.2 In The Affirmative.

6 28. Point No.3:

For the foregoing reasons C.C.No.2079/2020 and in view of the above findings, I pass the following:
ORDER
The accused is found guilty.
In Exercise of the Powers vested under section 255(2) of Cr.P.C., the accused is convicted for the offence punishable under section 138 of N.I.Act.
The accused is sentenced to pay fine amount of Rs.27,20,304/- (Twenty Seven Lakhs and Twenty Thousand Three Hundred Four Rupees Only)
In default of payment of fine, the accused shall undergo SI for six months.

In Exercise of the powers vested under Sec.357(1)(b) of Cr.P.C., out of the fine amount, the complainant is entitled for Rs.27,15,304/- (Twenty Seven Lakhs and Fifteen Thousand Three Hundred Four Rupees Only) towards compensation.

In Exercise of the powers vested under Sec.357(1) (a) of Cr.P.C.,
the remaining fine amount of Rs.5,000/- (Rupees Five Thousand only) is to be remitted to the state.
The personal bond executed by the accused shall stand cancelled and the cash security deposited by the accused shall be refunded to the accused after the appeal period is over.
A copy of the above judgment shall be supplied to the accused free of cost.
(Dictated to the Stenographer, transcribed and typed by her, corrected and signed and then pronounced by me in the open court on this the 09th day of May, 2025).
